strengths: Solid system design that tightly couples a dense correspondence-based visual front-end (inspired by DROID-SLAM) with IMU pre-integration in a unified optimization framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM.

Robust and well-designed three-stage IMU initialization (Pure Vision -> Inertial-only -> Joint VI) which successfully recovers scale and gravity direction, allowing the system to operate robustly on monocular datasets.

Efficient loop closure handling using Pose Graph Bundle Adjustment (PGBA) in Sim(3) combined with an elegant, closed-form Gaussian map update scheme. This maintains global consistency of the 3DGS map without needing expensive re-optimization or retraining from scratch.

Highly comprehensive experimental evaluation on four diverse datasets (EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, and FAST-LIVO2) under challenging conditions, including a detailed strided evaluation (simulating frame drops and high-speed motion) where the proposed method shows superior tracking stability and rendering quality.
weaknesses: The computational complexity of the system is high. Even with an ultra-high-end GPU (NVIDIA RTX 5090), the tracking and mapping system runs at around 4-11 FPS on some datasets, which limits its immediate applicability to embedded/robotic platforms with constrained hardware.

Individual algorithmic components rely heavily on existing work (such as DROID-SLAM for dense correspondences, standard IMU pre-integration, and PGBA from HI-SLAM2). The primary novelty is systemic integration and the specific Gaussian update formulation under loop closure, which makes the algorithmic contribution somewhat incremental.

There is a lack of technical discussion on how Sim(3) loop closures affect the physical metric scale and gravity alignment established by the IMU. When the trajectory is scaled/rotated via Sim(3) during loop closure, how are the velocity states and gravity direction corrected to ensure consistent subsequent IMU pre-integration?

Several baselines (like ORB-SLAM3, VINS-Mono, and OpenVINS) fail completely on the FAST-LIVO2 dataset (Table 5). The paper would benefit from a more detailed analysis explaining why these visual-inertial baselines failed (e.g., due to low frame rates, initialization errors, or specific motion patterns) while VIGS-SLAM succeeded.

strengths: Strong Tracking Performance and Robustness: The tightly coupled visual-inertial design significantly improves tracking accuracy (ATE) and robustness compared to both vision-only 3DGS SLAM methods (like HI-SLAM2, Splat-SLAM) and traditional visual-inertial SLAM systems (like ORB-SLAM3, VINS-Mono).

Excellent Performance Under Degraded Conditions: The strided evaluation and extreme condition experiments demonstrate that VIGS-SLAM handles frame drops, motion blur, and low-texture scenarios exceptionally well, maintaining tracking where other state-of-the-art pipelines fail.
High-Quality Reconstruction: VIGS-SLAM consistently delivers superior novel-view synthesis metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) across multiple challenging datasets.

Thorough Evaluation: The paper evaluates on four diverse datasets (EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, FAST-LIVO2), and provides comprehensive supplementary material with detailed per-sequence results and extensive ablation studies.
weaknesses: Limited Algorithmic Novelty: The core components are combinations of existing works. The visual front-end and dense bundle adjustment are directly based on DROID-SLAM, the IMU preintegration and staged initialization follow classic VIO designs (resembling VINS-Mono), and the PGBA loop closure and Gaussian update strategy are heavily inspired by HI-SLAM2. The integration is highly effective but represents more of an engineering/system contribution rather than introducing fundamentally new algorithmic concepts.

High Computational Overhead: Despite claiming 'real-time', the full system runs at only ~7 FPS on an extremely high-end NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU (as shown in Table 9). This heavy computational footprint restricts the system's current practicality for resource-constrained robotics or AR/VR mobile devices where visual-inertial SLAM is typically deployed.

Dependency on Learned Flow: Since the system heavily relies on DROID-SLAM's pretrained recurrent optical flow network, its generalization capabilities might be bounded by the training distribution of the flow model, although the tightly-coupled IMU constraints help mitigate tracking failures.

strengths: Tightly and robustly couples learning-based dense visual correspondences (derived from DROID-SLAM) with preintegrated inertial measurements, addressing tracking failures in visually degraded environments.
Proposes a practical staged IMU initialization scheme (pure vision, inertial-only with gravity/scale estimation, and joint visual-inertial refinement) to robustly boot the system.

Introduces an efficient Sim(3) Pose Graph Bundle Adjustment and an anchored Gaussian update strategy to preserve map consistency after loop closures without requiring complete re-optimization of the 3DGS map.

Conducts highly comprehensive experimental validation on four diverse datasets (EuRoC, RPNG, UTMM, FAST-LIVO2), including a rigorous strided evaluation to simulate frame drops and high-speed motion, where the proposed method shows outstanding tracking robustness.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental, as the visual-inertial tracking front-end closely follows the design of DROID-SLAM combined with standard preintegration formulations from classical VIO.

The processing speed is not fully real-time for the combined tracking and mapping system, running at around 4-11 FPS on a high-end RTX 5090 GPU (as shown in Table 9), which limits its deployability on resource-constrained robotic platforms.

The loop-closure Gaussian update assumes a simple rigid transformation and scaling of Gaussians anchored to keyframes, which might not fully resolve complex local deformations or non-uniform scale drift in very large-scale environments.
